text: Wildman Whitehouse applied 2,000 volts to the 1858 Atlantic cable to push signals through faster. Why could this never have worked, even if the insulation had survived?
choices: The cable's resistance was too high for any voltage to overcome
The limitation was intersymbol interference from the cable's capacitance, which more voltage makes taller rather than sharper
The receivers of the era could not detect signals above 1,000 volts
Seawater grounding dissipated any additional power applied
explanation: Thomson's law of squares described the real constraint: capacitance smears each pulse in time so successive pulses overlap. Raising the voltage scales the smeared pulse up without narrowing it, so the overlap is unchanged. The fix was a more sensitive receiver and a slower signalling rate, which is what Thomson supplied.
